title: Choose Comparison Criteria First
body:
Choosing comparison criteria first is the step that keeps a product or service comparison honest: the criteria are fixed before any option is looked at, so the winner cannot be chosen first and justified afterwards.

Method. First, write down what the purchase must do, in ordinary words. Second, turn each requirement into a criterion that can be checked, such as size, capacity, running cost, or warranty length. Third, mark which criteria are must-haves that rule an option out, and which are nice-to-haves that only rank the survivors. Fourth, only then collect the figures for each option, using the same unit for the same criterion every time.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for choose comparison criteria first. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: criteria: 5; must-have: fits the space, meets the capacity need; nice-to-have: running cost, warranty length, ease of repair Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this method whenever two or more options claim to do the same job. Do not use it to compare things built for different jobs, because a shared criterion list cannot be fair when the jobs differ, and do not add a new criterion after seeing the scores unless every option is re-scored on it. title: Total Cost Over Time, Not Just the Sticker Price
body:
Total cost over time is the honest price of a product or service: the upfront price plus every recurring charge, consumable, and expected repair over the period it will actually be used, compared over the same period for every option.

Method. First, fix the comparison period, such as two years. Second, list the upfront price. Third, add each recurring charge multiplied by the number of periods, and each consumable multiplied by how often it is replaced. Fourth, add any expected maintenance that the maker states. Fifth, compare the totals, not the upfront prices, and state the period alongside the total.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for total cost over time, not just the sticker price. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: upfront: 120; recurring: 180; consumables: 40; total over 12 months: 340 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this method for anything with running costs, subscriptions, or consumables. Do not use a total that mixes periods, such as one option over one year and another over three, and do not treat an expected repair as certain unless the record states why it is expected. title: Build a Side-by-Side Comparison Table
body:
A side-by-side comparison table puts every option in a column and every criterion in a row, so a missing figure shows up as an empty cell instead of quietly disappearing, and the reader can see exactly where each option wins and loses.

Method. First, list the options as columns. Second, list the criteria as rows, in the order fixed before scoring. Third, fill each cell with the same unit, or leave it blank and mark it unknown. Fourth, read down each column for the full picture of one option, and across each row for how all options compare on one criterion. Fifth, keep the source of each figure beside the table.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for build a side-by-side comparison table. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Option A total: 24; Option B total: 22; Option C total: 24; highest total: Option A Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this table for any choice with three or more criteria. Do not fill an unknown cell with a guess, and do not hide a weak row by dropping the criterion; a table that shows its gaps is more trustworthy than a table that hides them. title: Read a Specification Sheet Properly
body:
Reading a specification sheet properly means checking what each stated figure actually measures, what unit it uses, and what it leaves out, because two sheets can use the same word for different measurements and neither is lying.

Method. First, read the unit beside every figure. Second, check the conditions the figure was measured under, if stated. Third, list the figures that are missing and ask whether they matter for the job. Fourth, compare only figures measured the same way. Fifth, treat a single headline figure as a summary, never as the whole specification.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for read a specification sheet properly. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: stated: ['capacity', 'warranty_years', 'weight']; missing: ['running_cost']; complete: False Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this method before trusting any headline number. Do not compare a maximum figure from one sheet with a typical figure from another, and do not assume a missing figure is favourable; missing means unknown. title: Weight What Matters to You
body:
Weighting what matters turns a vague preference into an explicit score: each criterion gets a weight that says how much it counts, each option gets a score per criterion, and the weighted total shows which option fits this buyer's priorities, not a generic ranking.

Method. First, assign weights that add to ten, giving more to criteria that matter most. Second, score each option on each criterion on the same scale. Third, multiply each score by its weight and add the results. Fourth, read the result as a fit for these weights, and try a second set of weights to see whether the winner changes; if it does, the choice is genuinely close.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for weight what matters to you. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: weighted total A: 74; weighted total B: 74; winner: B Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use weighting when criteria conflict, so one option wins on price and another on durability. Do not present a weighted total without its weights, because the same scores give a different winner under different weights, and do not let a single criterion's weight swamp all the others without saying so. title: Check a Claim Against Its Source
body:
Checking a claim against its source means finding where a selling claim came from and whether the source actually says what the claim says, because a claim can be true in its source and misleading in the way it is quoted.

Method. First, copy the claim exactly. Second, find its stated source, or mark it unsourced if none is given. Third, read the source passage yourself and compare the numbers and the conditions. Fourth, note any change in unit, period, or condition between source and claim. Fifth, accept the claim only if source, numbers, and conditions all match.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for check a claim against its source. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: claim: 90; source: 90; numbers match: True; accepted: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this check for any claim that decides a purchase, especially a superlative claim such as best or fastest. Do not accept a claim that cites no source as if it were sourced, and do not accept a sourced claim whose conditions differ from the use at hand. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Read Reviews by Distribution, Not by Average Alone
body:
Reading reviews by distribution means looking at how ratings spread across the scale, not only at the average, because an average of four stars can hide a split between delighted and disappointed buyers, and a small number of reviews can make an average meaningless.

Method. First, count the reviews. Second, count how many fall at each star level. Third, read the average only alongside that count and spread. Fourth, read a sample of the lowest and highest reviews, not only the most recent. Fifth, ask whether the reviewers describe the same use as yours.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for read reviews by distribution, not by average alone. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: review count: 10; average: 4.0; stars 1 : 1; stars 2 : 1; stars 3 : 0; stars 4 : 3; stars 5 : 5 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use distribution reading for every reviewed product or service. Do not trust an average built on very few reviews as if it were built on many, and do not ignore a large minority of low ratings just because the average looks good. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Spot Manipulated Reviews Without Accusing Anyone
body:
Spotting manipulated reviews means looking for patterns that make a review set less trustworthy, such as many near-identical short reviews in a burst, or reviews that praise features the product does not have, and then lowering trust in the set rather than accusing any named seller.

Method. First, look at the timing and wording of reviews together. Second, count how many reviews are very short and generic versus specific about the actual use. Third, check whether negative reviews receive replies that address the point. Fourth, compare the review picture with at least one independent source. Fifth, if the pattern is strong, treat the whole set as weak evidence and rely on other checks instead.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for spot manipulated reviews without accusing anyone. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: reviews: 5; identical generic: 3; generic share: 0.6 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use pattern checks before trusting any review set. Do not accuse a named seller of manipulation on the basis of a pattern alone, and do not discard genuine enthusiastic reviews just because they are short; the pattern, not a single review, is the signal. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Verified Reviews, Incentives, and Disclosures
body:
Verified reviews, incentives, and disclosures are the labels that tell a reader whether the reviewer actually bought or used the item, whether they were given something for the review, and whether that fact is stated plainly, so the reader can weigh the review accordingly.

Method. First, check the verified or confirmed-purchase label where the platform provides one. Second, look for a disclosure of a free item, discount, or payment. Third, weigh an undisclosed-incentive review lower than a plainly disclosed one, and a disclosed one lower than an independent one. Fourth, remember that verification proves a purchase, not honesty or expertise. Fifth, keep the incentive question separate from whether the review describes the actual use well.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for verified reviews, incentives, and disclosures. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: reviews: 4; verified: 3; with disclosed incentive: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use incentive and verification labels on every review set. Do not treat verified as meaning truthful, and do not treat an incentivised review as automatically false; the label changes the weight, it does not settle the truth. title: Compare Service Quotes Line by Line
body:
Comparing service quotes line by line means matching each charge in one quote against the same work in another, because two quotes for the same job can differ in what is included, what is charged separately, and what is left out entirely.

Method. First, list every line of the first quote. Second, find the matching line in the second quote, or mark it missing. Third, add the lines that cover the same work and compare those subtotals. Fourth, list separately charged items and exclusions for each quote. Fifth, ask the provider to confirm any line that is unclear before choosing on price.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for compare service quotes line by line. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: quote A total: 500; quote B total: 460; parts difference: -30 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use line-by-line comparison for contractors, repairers, insurers, and professionals. Do not compare headline totals when the included work differs, and do not assume the cheapest headline is the cheapest like-for-like job. title: Compare Trial, Return, and Warranty Terms
body:
Comparing trial, return, and warranty terms means reading the conditions that apply after purchase, because a lower price with a short return window and a short warranty can cost more than a higher price with generous terms, especially for items that fail early.

Method. First, note the trial or cooling-off period and its conditions. Second, note the return window, who pays return costs, and what condition the item must be in. Third, note the warranty length and what it excludes. Fourth, note how a claim is made and how long it takes. Fifth, compare the whole terms package, not one term alone.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for compare trial, return, and warranty terms. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: return days A: 30; return days B: 14; warranty years A: 2; warranty years B: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use terms comparison whenever the item may not suit or may fail. Do not assume terms are the same because prices are similar, and do not ignore an exclusion that covers exactly the failure you are worried about. title: When a Comparison Cannot Decide
body:
When a comparison cannot decide, the honest result is a tie or an unknown, not a forced winner: two options can score equally, the deciding criterion can be unmeasured, or the available evidence can be too thin, and naming that state protects the buyer from a false certainty.

Method. First, check whether the totals are genuinely close or equal. Second, check whether the deciding criterion is missing for one option. Third, check whether the evidence is thin enough that new evidence could reverse the result. Fourth, if any of these holds, record the result as undecided and state what evidence would decide it. Fifth, choose on a stated tie-breaker, such as terms or availability, and say that it is a tie-breaker, not a quality verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for when a comparison cannot decide. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: scores: {'Option A': 24, 'Option B': 24}; tie: True; verdict: undecided - tie, decide on terms Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use the undecided result whenever the evidence does not support a winner. Do not force a winner to make a comparison look complete, and do not treat a tie-breaker choice as proof that the chosen option is better. title: Compare Used Against New
body:
Comparing used against new means pricing the used option's remaining life, condition, and risk alongside its lower price, because a used item can be the better buy or a false saving depending on how much useful life remains and what a failure would cost.

Method. First, state the new price and expected life. Second, state the used price, age, and condition as reported. Third, estimate remaining life from age and condition, and say it is an estimate. Fourth, add expected repair or replacement costs for the used option over that remaining life. Fifth, compare cost per year of remaining life, not purchase price alone.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for compare used against new. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this comparison for durable goods and equipment. Do not compare a used price with a new price without adjusting for remaining life, and do not treat a seller's condition description as an inspection. title: Long-Term Ownership Costs
body:
Long-term ownership costs are the maintenance, consumables, energy, and eventual replacement that a product or service accrues over its whole life, and they often outweigh the purchase price, which is why a cheap purchase can be the expensive choice.

Method. First, list every recurring ownership cost and its interval. Second, multiply each by how often it falls inside the ownership period. Third, add the purchase price. Fourth, add any stated disposal or exit cost. Fifth, compare the lifetime totals over the same ownership period and state the assumptions behind each figure.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for long-term ownership costs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: purchase: 200; yearly running: 50; lifetime total: 450 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use lifetime costing for appliances, vehicles, tools, and subscriptions. Do not compare lifetime costs built on different periods or different assumption sets, and do not omit a known recurring cost because it is small in one year; small yearly costs grow over a long life. title: Combine Review Sources Without Double-Counting
body:
Combining review sources without double-counting means merging ratings from several platforms while removing the same review counted twice and weighting each source by its review count, so a single enthusiastic source cannot masquerade as many independent sources.

Method. First, list each source with its review count and average. Second, check whether the same reviews appear on more than one platform and remove duplicates where they can be identified. Third, combine by weighting each average by its count. Fourth, report the combined count and the spread of the source averages. Fifth, if the sources disagree widely, report the disagreement instead of hiding it in one number.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for combine review sources without double-counting. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: combined reviews: 50; combined average: 4.12 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use combined ratings only when the sources measure the same thing on the same scale. Do not average averages without weighting by count, and do not combine sources that review different versions or uses as if they were one. title: Record the Decision and Why
body:
Recording the decision and why means writing down the options, the criteria, the scores, the terms, and the reason for the final choice, so the decision can be checked later, learned from, and defended if the outcome disappoints.

Method. First, write the decision in one sentence. Second, list the criteria and weights used. Third, record the scores or figures for the top two options. Fourth, record the terms that mattered and any evidence that was missing. Fifth, note the date and the conditions under which the decision should be revisited.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for record the decision and why. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: choice: Option B; reason: lower lifetime total; missing evidence: long-term reliability Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use a decision record for any purchase that matters, especially one that will be lived with for years. Do not write the record after the outcome is known and backdate the reasoning; a record written before the outcome is the one that teaches.
